newsitem.title: UK: IRA suspected of blast claimed by shadowy group.
newsitem.headline: IRA suspected of blast claimed by shadowy group.

text.p: Britain on Tuesday pointed an accusing finger at the IRA for a car bomb attack inside its Northern Ireland army headquarters, one of the most heavily guarded installations in Western Europe.

A caller to Irish radio claimed the explosions on Monday were the work of a shadowy Irish Republican group, the Continuity Army Council (CAC), but failed to give a password used previously to authenticate bomb claims and warnings in messages to media and security forces.

The group abandoned a 250 lb (120 kg) car bomb in Belfast last week which was destroyed. It also claimed credit for a July car bomb against a Northern Ireland hotel but its failure to use a coded password cast doubt on the callers' claims.

Security sources believe it is linked to the Republican Sinn Fein (RSF) party, which broke from the mainstream Irish Republican movement in the 1970s in a row about whether or not republicans should contest British elections. RSF denies having a military arm.
Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew said after a briefing from army and police security chiefs that the attack bore the hallmarks of the Irish Republican Army (IRA).
He told a news conference that the Lisburn bombing in which two car bombs went off was "consistent with a terrorist organisation which declared a ceasefire in August, 1994".

The IRA, which wants to end rule by Britain, called a truce in August 1994 to try to get its Sinn Fein political wing invited to all-party peace talks but went back to war in February against British targets outside Northern Ireland.

The Lisburn attack was the first against British troops in the province since the IRA ceasefire and raised the spectre of violence by vengeful Protestant "Loyalist" groups which have abided by their own two-year truce until now.

Army chiefs began an immediate review of security at their Lisburn army headquarters where bombers detonated two car bombs injuring 20 soldiers and 11 civilians and jolting a two-year Anglo-Irish attempt to forge a peace settlement.

The IRA itself stayed silent on widespread allegations that it was behind the meticulously organised attack. In the past it has quickly either denied or claimed such incidents. Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams brushed aside questions about possible IRA involvement and extended his sympathy to the victims, 12 of whom were still in hospital, three with serious injuries, 24 hours after the attack.
He insisted he was ready to take part in the peace talks, from which his party is barred as punishment for the IRA decision to end its 17-month truce.

There was no sign that either Britain or Ireland would abandon their insistence on an end to IRA violence as a condition of Sinn Fein's entry into the talks, nor that they might abandon the negotiations, which have faltered since opening in June.
"No consideration has been given to postponing the talks," Irish Prime Miniser John Bruton told the Irish Parliament.
The British and Irish governments said they would press ahead with the peace talks and appealed to Loyalists, who have killed 900 Catholics to avenge IRA attacks, to keep their truce.

"There's no doubt whoever planted these devices were intent to try to blow the process that is taking place at the moment out of the water and any challenge to a democratic process of that kind must be resisted," Britain's junior Northern Ireland Minister Michael Ancram told the BBC.
"I call on particularly the Loyalist paramilitaries not to fall into the trap of those who planted those devices with murderous intent and maintain their ceasefire," he said.
